mappings.note: What a galaxy is, and the Milky Way described as it appears in a dark sky. Defining a class of system and placing ours in it, LO-133.
The challenges of sky watching and at least three preparations -- dark site, moonless night, thirty minutes of dark adaptation. Planning an observation, LO-134.
The Chandrayaan missions, the south-pole landing and the sample-return aim of Chandrayaan-4. Space science as applied achievement; LO-140 is the nearest fit in a frame with no LO for missions.
Saptarishi identified as the Big Dipper and its pointers used to find Polaris (LO-131), with part (iii) asking why that star guides a night traveller (LO-140).
Venus after sunset: parts (ii) and (iii) both turn on how planets differ from stars -- steady light, reflected rather than generated. An explicit differentiation, LO-132.
A rocky irregular body between Mars and Jupiter is an asteroid in the asteroid belt; an icy one with a tail would be a comet. Sorting bodies into classes, LO-133.
Chandrayaan-3 at the lunar south pole. LO-140 for the mission and why the site matters, LO-135 for part (iii), which asks how the absent atmosphere changes the landing.

The Hanle Dark Sky Reserve and the Milky Way overhead. LO-133 for naming the galaxy and what galaxies contain, LO-141 for part (iii), which asks why a reserve with minimal light pollution makes it visible.
